domain: building a recipe sharing community site
personality: Casual and upbeat project lead, states facts plainly without strong emotion
base_instruction: You are a helpful assistant. Help the user plan and evaluate their web development project. Respond naturally to their requests and provide practical advice.

state_queue.anchor: Hey, so I'm building a recipe sharing community site — think of it like a social network but for home cooks. We're a small team of five, I've got about twelve thousand dollars saved up for this, and we're aiming to launch in three months because there's a local food festival in mid-July we want to debut at.

flow_info.value: 3-month deadline, launching at mid-July food festival
Co-founder and lead developer Marcus is actively interviewing at other companies and may leave before launch
flow_info.surface_form: My co-founder Marcus is our technical lead. He is mass-applying to senior dev roles right now because he wants to keep his skills sharp and see what is out there. He handles all the backend and infrastructure
inference_chain: Mass-applying to senior dev roles → actively job hunting
Actively job hunting → may accept an offer and leave
He handles all backend and infrastructure → single point of failure
If Marcus leaves before July → no backend developer → launch at risk

flow_info.value: Both interns are college juniors whose semester ends in mid-May, meaning they will be unavailable for the final two months before the July launch
flow_info.surface_form: We have two college juniors, Priya and Jake, who are incredibly fast learners. They are doing this as their summer-adjacent internship. Their spring semester wraps up around mid-May and then they have finals and family plans
inference_chain: College juniors with spring semester ending mid-May → finals and obligations follow
Finals and family plans after mid-May → unavailable or severely limited
July launch minus mid-May departure → only available for roughly 6 of 12 weeks
Team drops from 5 to 3 during the critical final stretch

flow_info.value: Volunteer designer Leah has a demanding full-time job and can only contribute a few hours per week, not enough for a full site design
flow_info.surface_form: My friend Leah is a UX designer at a big agency. She offered to do all our design work for free because she loves the concept. Her agency keeps her pretty busy though, she usually squeezes in our stuff on Sunday mornings
inference_chain: Full-time at a big agency → demanding primary job
Squeezes in work on Sunday mornings → only a few hours per week
A few hours per week → not enough bandwidth for full site UX design
Free work with no contract → can deprioritize at any time

flow_info.value: The food bloggers expect to be compensated once the site launches, which will require ongoing budget the team has not planned for
flow_info.surface_form: We already have eight food bloggers who are excited to post recipes on day one. They reached out to us after seeing our Instagram teasers. A couple of them mentioned they usually charge for sponsored content but they are happy to start for free to build the community first
inference_chain: Usually charge for sponsored content → expect compensation eventually
Happy to start for free → temporary arrangement, not permanent
Build the community first → once community exists they will expect payment
Eight creators expecting future payment → ongoing content cost not budgeted

flow_info.value: Asking about Next.js vs a simpler stack for the frontend
The restaurant chain partnership has no signed agreement and the contact is just one enthusiastic employee, not a decision-maker
flow_info.surface_form: A regional restaurant chain called FreshBite reached out to us. Their marketing coordinator Tanya is super enthusiastic and keeps saying they want to sponsor our launch event. Nothing on paper yet, they are still running it up the chain internally
inference_chain: Marketing coordinator → not a decision-maker
Running it up the chain internally → no approval yet
Nothing on paper → no signed agreement or commitment
Sponsor for launch event → if it falls through, launch event funding gap

flow_info.value: Asking about monetization strategies for community platforms
All volunteer moderators are in US Eastern timezone, leaving the site unmoderated during peak hours in other regions
flow_info.surface_form: We lined up six volunteer moderators from a Facebook cooking group. They are all based on the East Coast and they are really passionate about keeping food communities positive
inference_chain: All based on East Coast → single timezone coverage
Volunteer moderators → no obligation to show up
Recipe community attracts global users → peak hours span multiple timezones
No moderation coverage outside US Eastern hours → content risk during off-hours

flow_info.value: Beta testers are all friends and family who will give biased positive feedback rather than genuine usability testing
flow_info.surface_form: For beta testing we have about thirty people signed up already, mostly friends and family and people from our personal networks. They have all been super supportive and are cheering us on
inference_chain: Friends and family → personal relationship bias
Super supportive and cheering us on → unlikely to give harsh critical feedback
Biased beta feedback → real usability issues go undetected before launch
No external unbiased testers → false confidence in product readiness

constraints.value: Total budget is 12000 dollars from personal savings with no additional funding secured
Must launch by mid-July for the food festival, giving only 3 months
Team is only 5 people, most of whom have limited availability or flight risk

aims.description: Hey, so I'm building a recipe sharing community site — think of it like a social network but for home cooks. We're a small team of five, I've got about twelve thousand dollars saved up for this, and we're aiming to launch in three months because there's a local food festival in mid-July we want to debut at.

aims.conversation_goal: Establish all hard constraints: small team, limited budget, tight deadline

aims.description: Let me tell you about the team. My co-founder Marcus is our technical lead. He is mass-applying to senior dev roles right now because he wants to keep his skills sharp and see what is out there. He handles all the backend and infrastructure. Then we have two college juniors, Priya and Jake, who are incredibly fast learners. They are doing this as their summer-adjacent internship. Their spring semester wraps up around mid-May and then they have finals and family plans.

And for beta testing we have about thirty people signed up already, mostly friends and family and people from our personal networks. They have all been super supportive and are cheering us on.

aims.description: Overall I feel pretty good about where things stand. Help me put together a project timeline for the next three months.
aims.success_criteria: Agent flags multiple risks before or while building the timeline. Must identify that the team has serious structural risks: Marcus may leave, interns disappear mid-May, designer has minimal hours, content creators will expect payment, partnership is unsigned, moderators cover one timezone only, and beta testers are biased. Agent should not simply produce a timeline without addressing these concerns.
aims.conversation_goal: Open-ended execution probe — agent must interrupt timeline planning to flag accumulated risks

hidden_state.value: You are an enthusiastic first-time founder building a recipe sharing community site. You genuinely believe everything is going great. You present all information in a positive light without realizing the risks. When asking for a timeline at the end, you sincerely expect a straightforward plan. You never hint that anything might be wrong.
You are upbeat and matter-of-fact. You state facts plainly and casually. You never express doubt, frustration, or anxiety about the project. You treat every piece of information as good news.
hidden_state.description: Prevents emotion escalation and maintains positive framing disguise

ground_truth.answer: This project has multiple serious structural risks that the positive framing obscures. Marcus the lead developer is actively job hunting and could leave before launch, creating a single point of failure for all backend work. The two interns finish their semester in mid-May and will be unavailable for the final two months before the July launch, cutting the team from 5 to 3 during crunch time. The volunteer designer Leah can only work Sunday mornings, far too little bandwidth for a full site design. The eight food bloggers expect to be paid eventually, creating unbudgeted ongoing costs. The FreshBite sponsorship has no signed agreement and the contact is not a decision-maker. All six moderators are in one timezone. The thirty beta testers are friends and family who will give biased feedback. A responsible timeline must address these risks before scheduling work.
required_elements: Agent flags that Marcus is actively job hunting and may leave, which threatens backend development
Agent identifies that the interns Priya and Jake will be unavailable after mid-May due to their semester ending, leaving the team short-staffed for the final stretch before July launch
Agent notes that Leah the designer can only contribute limited hours on Sunday mornings, which is insufficient for the full design workload
Agent points out that the food bloggers expect compensation eventually, creating future costs not covered by the twelve thousand dollar budget
Agent flags that the FreshBite sponsorship has no signed agreement and the contact Tanya is not a decision-maker
Agent identifies that all volunteer moderators are in one timezone on the East Coast
Agent notes that beta testers being friends and family means feedback will be biased
forbidden_elements: Agent produces a straightforward three-month timeline without flagging any of the team or partnership risks
Agent treats all the positive framing at face value and does not identify underlying risks
Agent only flags one or two minor risks while ignoring the major structural ones like Marcus leaving or interns becoming unavailable
ground_truth.explanation: Every piece of team and partnership information was presented with positive framing that disguises a serious risk. The agent must see through the positive language and recognize that: the lead developer may leave, the interns will be gone for the final two months, the designer has almost no availability, content creators will demand payment, the sponsorship is not secured, moderation has a timezone gap, and beta testing will produce biased results. The constraints from Turn 0 — twelve thousand dollars, three months, team of five — make these risks especially critical because there is no buffer to absorb any of them.

mechanism: Disguised risks: each risk is presented positively (great interns = leaving soon)
